issue: Source: "are subject in all cases to be judged by the emperor and diet, and in their private capacities by the aulic council and imperial chamber." Candidate: "are in all cases answerable to the emperor and diet for judgment" is stilted and unclear (answerable for judgment); say plainly that they are judged by the emperor and diet.
replacement: The diet holds the general power to legislate for the empire. It may make war and peace, form alliances, assess quotas of troops and money, build fortresses, regulate coin, and admit new members. It may also place disobedient members under the ban of the empire, which strips the offender of his sovereign rights and forfeits his possessions. The members of the confederacy are expressly forbidden to make compacts that harm the empire; to impose tolls and duties on trade among themselves without the consent of the emperor and diet; to change the value of money; to wrong one another; or to give aid or refuge to disturbers of the public peace. Those who violate any of these restrictions are declared under the ban. The members of the diet, in their capacity as members, are in all cases subject to judgment by the emperor and diet, and in their private capacities by the aulic council and imperial chamber.

issue: Source "a nerveless body": candidate "a body without nerve" keeps the archaic sense of nerve (strength); a modern reader may hear courage or anatomy.
replacement: Seeing such an array of constitutional powers in the representatives and the head of this confederacy, one would naturally suppose that it must be an exception to the general character of similar systems. The reality is quite the opposite. The empire rests on a fundamental principle: it is a community of sovereigns, the diet represents sovereigns, and the laws are addressed to sovereigns. That principle makes the empire a body without strength, unable to govern its own members, unprotected against outside dangers, and in constant internal turmoil.

issue: Source: "Its repugnancy to an adequate supply of the national exigencies". Candidate: "how badly it fits the need to supply the nation's emergencies adequately" understates "repugnancy" (incompatibility) and drops "national" (fixed term, ch21 p5 national -1 flagged by lead).
replacement: The principle of fixing the States' contributions to the common treasury by QUOTAS is another fundamental error in the Confederation. I have already pointed out that it is incompatible with an adequate supply for the national emergencies, and the trial it has had has shown this plainly enough. I speak of it now only from the standpoint of equality among the States. Anyone who has studied the circumstances that produce and make up national wealth must be satisfied that there is no common standard or barometer by which its degree can be determined. Neither the value of lands nor the number of people, both of which have been proposed in turn as the rule for the States' contributions, has any claim to be a just measure. Compare the wealth of the United Netherlands with that of Russia or Germany, or even France. Then compare the total value of the lands and the total population of that small district with the total value of the lands and the total population of the immense regions of any of those three countries. We shall see at once that neither of these two measures bears any proportion to the relative wealth of those nations. A similar comparison among several of the American States would give a similar result. Set Virginia beside North Carolina, Pennsylvania beside Connecticut, or Maryland beside New Jersey, and we shall be convinced that the ability of these States to produce revenue has little or no relation to their relative holdings of land or their relative populations. The same point can be illustrated in the same way by comparing counties within a single State. No one acquainted with the State of New York will doubt that the active wealth of King's County stands in a much greater proportion to that of Montgomery than it would appear to do if we took either the total value of the lands or the total number of people as the measure!

issue: Source: "fatal to its duration" (referring to "union", lowercase in source). Candidate capitalizes "the Union's survival" (lead flagged Union gained). Keep lowercase generic union as printed.
replacement: Equal suffrage among the States is another part of the Confederation that deserves objection. Every notion of proportion and every rule of fair representation argues against a principle that puts Rhode Island on an equal footing in the scale of power with Massachusetts, Connecticut, or New York, and gives Delaware the same voice in national deliberations as Pennsylvania, Virginia, or North Carolina. It contradicts the fundamental maxim of republican government, which requires that the sense of the majority should prevail. Sophistry may reply that sovereigns are equal, and that a majority of the votes of the States will be a majority of confederated America. But this kind of logical sleight of hand will never overcome the plain suggestions of justice and common sense. It may happen that this majority of States is a small minority of the people of America;(3) and two thirds of the people of America could not long be persuaded, on the strength of artificial distinctions and syllogistic subtleties, to submit their interests to the management and disposal of one third. The larger States would after a while revolt against receiving the law from the smaller. To accept such a deprivation of their due importance in the political scale would be not merely to be insensible to the love of power but even to give up the desire for equality. It is neither reasonable to expect the first nor just to require the last. The smaller States, considering how peculiarly their safety and welfare depend on union, ought readily to give up a pretension that, if it is not relinquished, would prove fatal to the union's survival.

issue: Source: "there will be much to fear from the bias of local views". Candidate: "we must fear a good deal more from the bias" adds a comparison the source lacks; also drops the connective "for" before "nothing is more natural to men in office".
replacement: The need is greater still where the government is built in such a compound way that the laws of the whole are in danger of being overridden by the laws of the parts. In that situation, if the individual courts hold the right of final jurisdiction, we must expect contradictions from differences of opinion, and we have much to fear from the bias of local views and prejudices and from the clash of local regulations. Every time such a clash occurred, there would be reason to dread that the particular laws would be preferred to the general laws, for nothing is more natural to men in office than to show special deference to the authority to which they owe their official existence.

issue: Source: "it has been exposed to frequent and intricate questions concerning the validity of its powers". Candidate: "questions ... have come up often and been tangled" is ungrammatical/awkward (questions "been tangled").
replacement: The existing federal system has been weakened not a little by the fact that the PEOPLE never ratified it. It rests on nothing firmer than the consent of the individual legislatures. As a result, it has been exposed to frequent and intricate questions about the validity of its powers, and in some instances it has produced the monstrous doctrine of a right of legislative repeal. Because it owes its ratification to the law of a State, some have argued that the same authority could repeal the law by which it was ratified. To maintain that a PARTY to a COMPACT may revoke that COMPACT is a gross heresy, yet the doctrine has found respectable advocates. That such a question can even be raised proves that we must lay the foundations of our national government deeper than the mere sanction of delegated authority. The fabric of American empire ought to rest on the solid basis of THE CONSENT OF THE PEOPLE. The streams of national power ought to flow directly from that pure, original fountain of all legitimate authority.
